title: DESIGN
briefing: I make sure we don't run out of money before we run out of sky.
I make sure it doesn't melt, freeze or fall apart.
I make sure the data gets home.
I make sure it's worth it.
Two years. 2.5 million. One CubeSat to watch Sarawak's rainforest. We decide together.

nova: A reserve is a plan for surprises.
Let's check what the other departments need.
orion: Weigh it twice. Then write it down.
The battery has to carry the night.
juno: Healthy leaf, dry leaf. That is our question.
A clear target is worth waiting for.
kai: A beautiful image still has to get home.
Clouds above, rain at the dish. We plan for both.

dialogue: Sarawak plans its first satellite by 2030. Today, we start small.
A CubeSat. Shoebox size. It will watch our forests from space.
We have two years and a small budget. We need a team.
Welcome to Borneo Forest Watch. Our forests are our future.
This pilot and its Minister are fictional. The 2030 plan is our real-world context.
I make sure we don't run out of money before we run out of sky.
I make sure it doesn't melt, freeze or fall apart.
I make sure the data gets home.
I make sure it's worth it.
Each of you sees different gauges. Talk to each other.

beats.objective: Read the brief at the flight-plan terminal
dialogue: Welcome. Two years in orbit. 2.5 million to build our mission.
Carry an imager. Cover Sarawak. Return at least 70% of the data.
Stay inside the mass limit. Be ready in 24 months.
Talk to each other. All green before launch. Every choice costs something.
Mistakes teach us. Go to your departments, then come back for review.
Three ways up. Check the mass, cost and reliability together.
The launch choice sets the shape of the mission.
With rideshare, the rocket decides the orbit.
A dedicated launch lets us choose. Either way, check Sarawak coverage and life.
The jar is for surprises. We still have to fit inside 2.5 million.
A little room now can save a difficult choice later.
Start with the frame. The imager needs a place to live.
More room also means more mass and cost.
Face the panel toward the lamp. Watch the watt meter.
The array must run the loads and refill the battery.
Thirty-five minutes of shadow. The battery carries the night.
Survive the dark, then recharge before the next eclipse.
A thruster takes mass, power and money. It can also help us step aside.
Try the debris preview before you choose.
The launch limit is real. A margin leaves room for the final build.
Match the wave. A stronger link has its own costs.
Our camera makes data. Our radio has to bring it home.
Start with Kuching. Check what another dish would add.
Reach 70% data returned, and keep an eye on the budget.

beats.objective: Mei Ling: schedule the downlink passes
dialogue: The pass windows are short. The data tank is not endless.
I'll fit the downlink blocks into the passes before the tank overflows.
Healthy leaf, dry leaf. The imager sees the difference.
Red, near-infrared and thermal help us ask different questions.
The imager is required. Calibrate it before adding anything else.
There is room for ambition, if the bay, mass and power allow it.
Pack the payload. Check the limits as you go.
Wide is coarse. Narrow is sharp. Both have a use.
We need a useful view of Sarawak, with a plan for clouds.
Let's put the imaging slots in clearer months.
Respect the data and power caps. Leave room for weather.

beats.objective: Bring the design to the Mess Hall
dialogue: The department choices are on the table. Now they have to fit together.
Design recorded. Next comes integration review.
One small satellite. One shared plan. Bring every department to the review.
